title: Butchering a meat rabbit at home
subtitle: Skinning and jointing a rabbit from your own stock for the table.
excerpt: Home-reared rabbit is lean, fine-grained, and well suited to braises, pies, and ragù. Butchering your own rabbit allows you to use every part and know the provenance completely. The process from freshly dispatched carcass to dressed rabbit takes 15 to 20 minutes with practice. Here is the skinning and jointing sequence.
sourceNotes: John Seymour, The Self-Sufficient Life and How to Live It (2009), rabbit husbandry chapter. FARMA, home slaughter and butchery guidance for smallholders. River Cottage Meat Book (Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall, 2004), rabbit section.

glossaryTerms.definition: A rabbit that has been skinned and eviscerated (gutted) but not jointed. The dressed carcass includes the back legs, saddle, and front legs. Dressed weight is typically 50–60% of live weight.

content.text: A freshly dispatched rabbit should be paunched (gutted) within an hour of killing to prevent digestive contamination affecting the meat. A clean
rabbit hangs for 24 to 48 hours in a cool larder or fridge before butchering to allow rigor to pass and the fibres to relax.
Hang the rabbit by its back legs from a hook, or lay it on a clean board. Remove the head if not already done.
Cut through the skin around each back hock. Pull the skin down over the legs toward the body; it will peel away from the muscle with light pulling.
Continue pulling the skin down over the body in one piece toward the front legs. Peel it over the front legs and finally over the neck stump.
The skin comes off whole. Freeze or salt the pelt immediately if you intend to tan it; otherwise discard.
Make a shallow cut through the belly skin from the base of the sternum to the pelvis, using the tip of the knife and keeping the blade angled away from the gut.
Pull the gut sac out in one movement, holding the intestines away from the meat. Cut the gut free at the rectum and esophagus.
Remove the liver (keep it: it is excellent), kidneys, and heart. Discard the rest.
Rinse the body cavity briefly under cold water, dry, and refrigerate for 24 hours before jointing.

Joint the rabbit into: two back legs (cut through the hip joint), the saddle (the loin section, cut between the last rib and the pelvis), and two front shoulders (pulled away from the ribcage or cut through the shoulder joint). The ribcage can be used for stock or discarded. A standard rabbit gives four to five portions from these joints.
